g1.correct: International student numbers have risen sharply since 2015.
accept: International student numbers have risen sharply since 2015.
g1.label: 1. International student numbers in Country A rose from 40,000 in 2015 to 95,000 in 2023.
g1.why: More than doubling over eight years is a big change, so “has risen sharply” is correct — not “fallen” (the numbers went up) or “fluctuated” (there is one clear direction, not ups and downs).

g2.correct: The number of temporary work visas has risen gradually over five years.
accept: The number of temporary work visas has risen gradually over five years.
g2.label: 2. The number of temporary work visas issued grew slowly but steadily, from 22,000 to 27,000, over five years.
g2.why: A slow, steady rise over five years is a gradual increase — “gradually” fits a slow change, unlike “fallen” (the number rose) or “remained exactly the same” (it did change, just slowly).

g3.correct: Asylum applications have fallen sharply in the last two years.
accept: Asylum applications have fallen sharply in the last two years.
g3.label: 3. Asylum applications fell from 60,000 to 12,000 in just two years.
g3.why: Dropping from 60,000 to 12,000 in two years is a big, fast fall, so “has fallen sharply” is correct — not “risen” (the numbers went down) or “remained stable” (they changed a great deal).

g4.correct: Family visas have fallen slightly over three years.
accept: Family visas have fallen slightly over three years.
g4.label: 4. Family visas dropped slightly, from 34,000 to 31,000, over three years.
g4.why: A small drop of 3,000 over three years is a slight fall, not a sharp one — and it is a fall, not a rise or an unpredictable fluctuation.

g5.correct: Net migration has remained stable for the whole decade.
accept: Net migration has remained stable for the whole decade.
g5.label: 5. Net migration stayed at almost exactly 200,000 a year for the whole decade.
g5.why: Staying at almost exactly the same figure for ten years is the definition of “remained stable” — not a sharp rise or a slight fall, since the figure barely moved at all.

g6.correct: The number of returning citizens has fluctuated from year to year.
accept: The number of returning citizens has fluctuated from year to year.
g6.label: 6. The number of returning citizens went up and down unpredictably every year, with no clear pattern.
g6.why: Going up and down with no clear pattern is exactly what “fluctuated” describes — unlike “risen steadily” or “remained completely stable”, both of which describe a single, consistent direction.

g7.correct: New arrivals peaked in 2020 before falling sharply the following year.
accept: New arrivals peaked in 2020 before falling sharply the following year.
g7.label: 7. New arrivals climbed every year until 2020, then dropped suddenly the following year.
g7.why: A rise followed by a high point and then a sudden drop is a classic “peaked … before falling” pattern — the numbers did not stay stable, and they did not fall gradually before 2020 and then rise.

accept: Student visas have increased marginally.
g8.label: 8. Student visas issued increased only very slightly, from 18,000 to 19,200.
g8.why: A rise of only 1,200 out of 18,000 is a very small increase, so “marginally” fits — not “dramatically” (the change is tiny) or “decreased” (the number went up, not down).

g1.correct: Just under half of respondents gave family reasons.
accept: Just under half of respondents gave family reasons.
g1.label: 1. Of 1,000 people surveyed, 480 gave family reasons for migrating (48%).
g1.why: 48% is a little less than 50%, so “just under half” is the accurate description — not “the vast majority” (well over half) or “a small minority” (well under half).

g2.correct: Roughly two-thirds of arrivals came for work.
accept: Roughly two-thirds of arrivals came for work.
g2.label: 2. Of 1,000 arrivals, 670 came for work (67%).
g2.why: 67% is close to two-thirds (about 66.7%), so “roughly two-thirds” is the best fit — it is well above “just under half” and far too high to be “a small minority”.

g3.correct: Roughly a third of the refugees resettled were children.
accept: Roughly a third of the refugees resettled were children.
g3.label: 3. Of 600 refugees resettled, 200 were children (33%).
g3.why: 200 out of 600 is exactly one third, so “roughly a third” is correct — not “the majority” (well over half) or “almost none” (a much smaller share).

g4.correct: City A received more than twice as many migrants as City B.
accept: City A received more than twice as many migrants as City B.
g4.label: 4. City A received 40,000 migrants last year; City B received only 16,000.
g4.why: 40,000 is more than double 16,000 (double would be 32,000), so “more than twice as many … as” is the accurate comparison — the two figures are not close, and City A received more, not fewer.

g5.correct: The vast majority of new residents said they planned to stay permanently.
accept: The vast majority of new residents said they planned to stay permanently.
g5.label: 5. 9 out of 10 new residents surveyed said they planned to stay permanently (90%).
g5.why: 90% is a very high proportion, so “the vast majority” fits best — far higher than “roughly half” and the opposite of “a minority”.

g6.correct: Only a small minority of arrivals surveyed were over 65.
accept: Only a small minority of arrivals surveyed were over 65.
g6.label: 6. Only 60 of the 1,000 arrivals surveyed were over the age of 65 (6%).
g6.why: 6% is a very small share, so “a small minority” is correct — nowhere near “the majority” or “exactly half”.

g7.correct: Work-related visas accounted for the largest share of all visas issued.
accept: Work-related visas accounted for the largest share of all visas issued.
g7.label: 7. Work-related visas made up 55% of all visas issued — more than any other single category.
g7.why: Being the biggest single category at 55% means work-related visas “accounted for the largest share” — the text is about work-related visas being biggest, not family visas, and 55% is the largest share, not the smallest.

accept: for
g8.label: 8 (review) — “It was surprising ___ researchers to find that migration figures had barely changed.”
g8.why: Review from 10g-digital-footprint: “surprising” comments on the situation itself (like “easy” or “important”), so it takes “for” — “of” is used after adjectives that judge someone's behaviour (careless, kind), which is not the case here.
